newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian premier regrets Italian statement.
newsitem.headline: Albanian premier regrets Italian statement.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino said on Wednesday he regretted Italy's threat to withdraw its troops if elections planned for June were postponed and said he was optimistic about resolving a political dispute over a new electoral law.
Speaking after meeting European envoy Franz Vranitzky, Fino appealed to Albanian President Sali Berisha to compromise in the dispute.

"This is the last chance for all of us Albanians, not only to get out of the crisis but to see the future of our country, especially the building of institutions, the rule of law and a powerful market economy," he told reporters.

Fino said he regretted Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta's statement to parliament in Rome that the Italian-led multinational force in Albania to secure humanitarian aid supplies should be withdrawn if the all-party agreement to hold elections was broken.

"I regret such a statement, but I want to emphasise that I'm quite optimistic today after the meeting I had with Mr Vranitzky about the possibility of reaching a consensus (on the electoral law)," he said.
Vranitzky, a former Austrian chancellor now acting as envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), met Fino shortly after arriving on a three-day visit.
It was his third since widespread rioting over failed pyramid savings schemes pushed Albania to the brink of anarchy in March.
"There should not be obstacles that can not be overcome by finding a compromise here in Albania," the European envoy said.
"I see there are possibilities which have to be elaborated on in the next couple of days."

Vranitzky said he would convey to President Berisha and other political leaders in Albania "the expectation of the international community that they find political consensus as far as the election is concerned".

Fino repeated his threat to resign unless the Albanian parliament, dominated by Berisha's Democratic Party, passes the new law increasing the number of seats to be elected by proportional representation.

"The electoral law is an essential law. And if my government does not receive a vote of confidence on this law that means that it does not have a vote of confidence to rule. I think it is high time to get used to this practice even in Albania," he said.
Fino's Socialist Party and the Democratic Party have failed in five meetings to agree on the election law.

The Italian threat came as a shock to Albanians, many of whom are hoping the mandate of the 6,000-strong eight-nation force will be extended to allow it to provide security for the election and ensure it is free and fair.

The Socialists withdrew from last May's elections late on polling day, complaining of fraud. International monitors agreed that the vote, which gave Berisha's party 122 seats in the 140-seat parliament, was seriously flawed.
The election deadlock must be resolved over the next few days if the vote is to be held on schedule.
Albanian law requires the president to issue a decree calling the election at least 45 days before it is held, meaning he has another eight days if the vote is to take place by June 29.
